body.translated_text:
Composed by <s>Paṇḍitāśoka</s>.
<s>Avayavinirākaraṇam</s> (Refutation of the Composite Whole).

children.translated_text: Such an excess of practice has not been undertaken, nor has such learning been acquired;
yet if I, with rashness, now endeavor to fashion even a fragment of meaning,
let all this, having been considered, be examined by the learned as it has been stated;

children.text: prīṇantyeva vi + + + + hi śiśoḥ prāyaḥ pitṛṇāṃ manaḥ //
children.translated_text: for indeed, the [even faltering] . . . of a child generally delight the minds of parents.

body.text: yo virudvadharmmādhyāsavān nāsāvekaḥ / yathā ghaṭādirarthaḥ / virudvadharmmādhyāsavāṃśca sthūlonīlādirartha iti vyāpakavirudvopalabdhiḥ / iha dṛśyamānasthūlonīlādirartho dharmmī, sa cānubhavāvasito 'sati bādhake pratyakṣasidvo hetorāśrayāsidviṃ nihanti / nanu bhavadbhirasannevāvayavī pratijñāyate sa kathaṃ pratyakṣasidvaḥ / nāvayavinamiha dharmmiṇaṃ pratipannāḥ smaḥ kintu pratibhāsamānasthūla nīlādikamartham / na tarhi virudvadharmmasaṃsargādavayavina ekatvaṃ niṣidvaṃ syāt / yadyevaṃ kastarhi bhavato 'vayavī / eko 'nekāvayavasamavetārtha iti cet / sa kiṃ pratibhāsamānāt sthūlanīlāderanyo 'nanyo vā / na tāvaṃdanyaḥ, dṛśyatvenābhyupagamāt / na ca pratibhāsamānasthūlanīlārthavyatirekeṇāparaḥ pratibhāti / ananyaścet / tasyaikatvapratikṣepe kathamapratiṣidvamekatvamavayavinaḥ /
body.translated_text: That which has the superimposition of contradictory properties is not a single entity — like a pot and such objects. And the gross object of blue and the like does have the superimposition of contradictory properties — this is an apprehension of contradiction in what is pervaded. Here, the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) is the perceptually apparent gross object of blue and such; and that, being ascertained through experience, in the absence of a sublating cognition, is established by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception), which defeats the [charge of] unestablished locus for the reason. Objection: Since you declare that the <s>avayavin</s> (composite whole) simply does not exist, how is it established by perception? Reply: We do not accept the <s>avayavin</s> as the <s>dharmin</s> here; rather, [we accept] the appearing gross blue object and the like. Then the oneness of the <s>avayavin</s> would not be refuted through its association with contradictory properties. If so, then what is the <s>avayavin</s> for you? If it is said to be a single entity inherent in many parts — is that other than or non-different from the appearing gross blue object? It is not other, since it is accepted as visible. And no other [entity] appears apart from the appearing gross blue object. If non-different, then when the oneness of that [gross object] is refuted, how is the oneness of the <s>avayavin</s> not refuted?

body.text: nanu ca pratibhāsamānaścedarthonāvayavirūpodharmmī / kintarhi rūpamasyāvaśiṣṭaprasidvaṃ bhaviṣyatīti / ucyate, pratibhāsamānaḥ sthūlonīlākāraḥ pratyakṣasidvaṃ rūpaṃ, avayavitvānabhyupagame 'pyavaśiṣyate / na caivaṃ mantavyaṃ / na paramāṇusañcayavādināṃ sthūlākāraḥ kaścidartho 'sti yaḥ prasidvo dharmmī syāditi / avayavyanabhyupagame 'pi hi niravayavānekātmakaḥ sthūlo 'rthobhyupagamyamānaḥ kena niṣidvaḥ / syānmataṃ niravayavāḥ paramāṇavaḥ kathaṃ pratyakṣe sthūlenā kāreṇāvabhāseran, sthūlasūkṣmayorvirodhāditi / tadapi na yuktaṃ / paramāṇava eva hi pararūpadeśaparihāreṇotpannāḥ parasparasahitā avabhāsamānā deśavitānavanto bhāsante / vitatadeśatvañca sthūlatvaṃ, yattuktaṃ sthūlasūkṣmayorvirodha iti tat kiṃ pararūpadeśaparihāravatī niravayavānāmutpattiḥ / parasparasahitānāmekavijñānāvabhāsitvaṃ vā virudvamiti vaktumadhyavasitaṃ / idañcedvirudvaṃ sthūlākāraḥ kiṃ virudvaḥ / ataeva niravayaveṣu bahuṣvekasmin vijñāne pratibhāsa māneṣu bhavan pratibhāsakālabhāvī pratibhāsadharmmaḥ sthūlākāro na tu vāstavaḥ pratyekamabhāvāt / pratibhāsāt prāgūrdvaṃ vā na tarhi sthūlo 'rtha iti cet / na tadāpi pratibhāsayogyatāsambhavāt yadaiva hi sañcitā bhaveyustadaiva pratibhāsayogyāḥ paramāṇavaḥ / yadā ca pratibhāsayogyā stadā sthūlāḥ / yastvāha niravayaveṣu bahuṣu pratibhāsamāneṣvavaśyamantareṇāpi pratibhāsitavyaṃ / antarānavabhāse parasparaviviktā eva nāvabhāsitāḥ syuḥ / viviktānavabhāse cāṇumātrakaṃ piṇḍo bhavet / na cāntaramavabhāsamānamutpaśyāmaḥ / tadayaṃ nirantara eka eva sthalo niravayavānekātmako bhavitumarhati, api tvekaḥ sthūlātmaka eveti / so 'pyevaṃ vācyaḥ / kiṃ vijātīyaparamāṇvantaramantaraṃ / āhosvit śūnyākāśayogaḥ / tatra śūnyākāśayogastāvadavastutayā nendriyapratyakṣagocaraḥ / arthasāmarthyabhāvini tātrārthasyaiva pratibhāsopapatteḥ / vijātīyantvindriyāntaragrāhyaṃ kathamindriyāntarajñāne 'vabhāsetāviṣayatvāt / tat kenāntareṇāvabhāsitavyamiti na vidmaḥ / yat punarucyate / antarālānavabhāse viviktā nāvabhāseranniti /
body.translated_text: Objection: If the appearing object is not of the form of an <s>avayavin</s> (composite whole), then the <s>dharmin</s> — what other well-established form will it have? Reply: The appearing gross blue form is a form established by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), and it remains even without accepting composite-wholeness. Nor should it be thought thus: 'For advocates of the aggregation of atoms, there is no gross-formed object that could serve as an established <s>dharmin</s>.' For even without accepting a composite whole, a gross object that is partless yet multiple in nature — by whom is it refuted [when thus accepted]? One might think: 'How can partless atoms appear in perception with a gross form, given the contradiction between gross and subtle?' But that too is not valid. For atoms themselves, having arisen without occupying the spatial location of others, appearing together with one another, manifest as having an extent of spatial location. And having extended spatial location is precisely grossness. As for the stated contradiction between gross and subtle — is it the arising of partless [atoms] while avoiding the spatial location of another's form, or is it the appearing of mutually associated [atoms] as a single cognition that is claimed to be contradictory? If this is contradictory, then how is a gross form contradictory? For this very reason, when many partless [atoms] appear in a single cognition, the gross form is a property of appearance existing at the time of appearance — not ultimately real, since it is absent in each [atom] individually. Objection: If before and after the appearance there is no gross object — Reply: Even then, the fitness for appearance is possible. For precisely when [atoms] are aggregated, atoms become fit for appearance. And when fit for appearance, they are gross. As for the claim that 'when many partless [atoms] appear, the intervening [space] too must necessarily appear — if the intervening [space] does not appear, they would appear only as mutually separated; and if separated [atoms] do not appear [as gross], the aggregate would be merely atom-sized; yet we do not observe the intervening [space] appearing — therefore this uninterrupted, single, gross [object] should not be partless and multiple in nature, but rather is a single gross entity' — to that too the response is as follows: Is the intervening [space] an atom of a different kind? Or is it a connection with empty space? As for empty space, being unreal, it is not an object of sensory perception. Since, when the object has causal power, the appearance of just that object is justified. But the heterogeneous [space-atom], being graspable by a different sense-faculty, how could it appear in the cognition of another sense-faculty, since it is not its object? Therefore, we do not know by what intervening [medium] it should appear. As for the further claim that 'if the intervening [space] does not appear, the separated [atoms] would not appear [as gross]' —

body.text: tatrāpi kimeṣāmantaraṃ vivekaḥ pararūpaśūnyatā veti cintyaṃ / nirūpayantastu pararūpaśūnyatāmeva vivekaṃ vastūnāṃ paśyāmaḥ / pararūpaśūnyāśceme bhāsamānāḥ kathaṃ viviktā nāvabhāseranniti / nanu ca na pratyekaṃ paramāṇūnāṃ sthūlākāraḥ / tataḥ samuditānāmeṣṭavyaḥ / yathā ca nīlaparamāṇūnāṃ pratyekamasambhavan pītākāro bahuṣvapi na dṛśyate / tathā pratyekamasambhavan sthūlākāraḥ kathaṃ bahuṣu syāditi /
body.translated_text: In that regard also, one must consider whether the distinctness of these [things] is their separation (<s>viveka</s>) or their emptiness of the form of another (<s>pararūpaśūnyatā</s>). Upon examination, we see that the distinctness of things is indeed their emptiness of the form of another. How could these, being empty of the form of another, yet appearing, not appear as distinct? Now, it is true that individual <s>paramāṇus</s> (atoms) do not have a gross form. Therefore, it must be sought in their aggregate. But just as the yellow appearance, which is impossible in individual blue <s>paramāṇus</s>, is not seen even in many [blue atoms], so how could a gross form, which is impossible in individual [atoms], exist in many?

body.text:
uktamatra / avirudvo niravayavāṇāṃ sthūlākāra iti / nīlavirudvastu pītākāraḥ / tataḥ pītavirudvaṃ nīlākāraṃ vibhrāṇeṣu bahuṣvapi kathaṃ pītākāro bhavet / naivaṃ niravayavatvavirudvaḥ sthūlākāraḥ yathoktānyāyāt / tadevaṃ pratyakṣasidvaḥ sthūlo 'rtha iha dharmmīti vyavasthitaṃ / tadevamavasthite dharmmiṇi hetoḥ sattvamasattvaṃ vā nirūpyaṃ / tatra pāṇyādāvekasmin kampamāne sthūlo 'rthaḥ sakampaniḥkampe rūpe yugapat pratipadyamānaḥ kathaṃ virudvadharmmasaṃsargavānna syāt / sakampaniḥkampayorhi rūpayoḥ parasparābhāvāvyabhicāranimittako 'sti virodhaḥ / bhāvābhāvayoreva hi parasparaparihārātmako virodhaḥ / vastunostu tadabhāvāvyabhicāreṇaiva / iha ca sakampaniḥkampe rūpe gṛhṇat pratyakṣameva sāmarthyāt parasparābhāvaṃ sādhayati / vyavahārayati tu nirvviśeṣaṇaivānupalabdhiḥ / syādetat pāṇyādāvekasminnavayave kampamāne nāvayavinaḥ kampa rūpamabhyupeyaṃ / avayava eva hi tadā kriyāvān dṛśyate / na cedaṃ mantavyaṃ / avayave kriyāvati tadādheyenāvayavināpi kriyāvatā bhavitavyaṃ, yathā rathe calati tadā rūḍho 'pi calatīti / avayavāvayavikarmmaṇorbhinnanimittatvāt / nimittāyaugapadyācca / yadā hi ātmanaḥ pāṇikampanecchā bhavati / tataḥ prayatnaḥ / tadā prayatnavadātmapāṇisaṃyogāt pāṇau kriyā / yadā tu śarīrakampanārthaḥ prayatnaviśeṣa ātmano jāyate / tadā tatprayatnavadātmaśarīrasaṃyogāt śarīre karmmeti nimittabhedaḥ / ato bhinnamiti tayorekasmin jāte kathaṃ nimittāntarapratibadvajanmā tadabhāve tadaparo 'pi tathaiva jāyeta / ratha tadārūḍhakarmmaṇostu satyapi nimittabhede nimittayaugapadyāt sahabhāvaḥ / tathā hi nodanaṃ rathakarmmaṇo 'samavāyikāraṇaṃ / tadārūḍhakarmmaṇastu nodyasaṃyogaḥ / tayośca sahabhāvāt karmmaṇī api yaugapadyena jāyete / tadetat sakalamālocya bhadantadharmmottareṇedamuktam / na cātrā vayavaḥ kriyāvān / avayaveṣu hi kriyāvatsu vibhāgo jāyate / kriyāyā vibhāgārambhaṃ prati nirapekṣakāraṇatvāt / tena ca saṃyoge 'samavāyikāraṇe nivarttate nivarttetāvayavi dravyamiti / idamāhuratra kaṇādaśiṣyāḥ / nodanādabhighātādvā jāyamānaḥ kriyāviśeṣo dravyārambhakasaṃyogapratidvandvivibhāgārambhako dṛṣṭaḥ / anyattu vibhāgamātramārabhate na tu yathoktaviśeṣaṃ / anyasmin padmasaṅkocavikāśādike karmmaṇyavayavasaṃyoganivṛtteradarśanāt / tadvat prayatnajanyasyāpi karmmaṇo nāsti saṃyoganivarttanasāmarthyaṃ / tato nāsti dravyanivṛttiriti
/ ayamatra samādhiḥ / ihāvayavini kriyāvati niyamenāvayavairapi kriyāvadbhirbhavitavyaṃ / anyathāvayavasaṃsṛṣṭebhya ākāśadeśebhyo vibhāgo 'vayavāsaṃsṛṣṭeśca saṃyogovayavinaḥ kriyāvataḥ syāt / avayavāstu kriyāvirahiṇaḥ pūrvvakrāntebhyo nabhodeśebhyo nāpasaryyeyuḥ / avayavisamākrāntaiśca deśairnābhisambadhyeran / na cāvayavisaṃyogavibhāgābhyāmavayavasaṃyogavibhāgau vācyau / kāryyasaṃyogavibhāgayoḥ kāraṇasaṃyogavibhāgau prati nimittabhāvānabhyupagamāt / kāraṇasaṃyogavibhāgāveva hi kāryyasaṃyogavibhāgāvārabhete /
body.translated_text: It has been stated here: the gross form is not contradictory for partless [atoms]. But the yellow form is contradictory for blue. Therefore, even in the presence of many [atoms] bearing a form contradictory to yellow, how could a yellow form arise? It is not so — the gross form is not contradictory to partlessness, by the principle already stated. Thus it is established that the gross object, proven by direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), is the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) here. With the property-bearer thus established, the existence or non-existence of the reason (<s>hetu</s>) must be determined. In this regard, when one part such as the hand is moving, the gross object — cognizing simultaneously both the moving and the non-moving form — how could it not possess a conjunction of contradictory properties? For between the moving and non-moving forms, there is a contradiction grounded in the invariable absence of each in the presence of the other. For contradiction is of the nature of mutual exclusion between existence and non-existence alone. But for a real thing, it is through the invariable absence of that [counterpart]. And here, direct perception itself, grasping the moving and non-moving forms, establishes by its own power the mutual absence [of each in the other]. It is the unqualified non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) that governs practical usage. [Objection:] One need not accept that when a single part such as the hand is moving, the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) has the form of movement. For it is only the part that is then seen to have action. [Reply:] This should not be maintained. When the part has action, the composite whole resting on it must also have action — just as when the chariot moves, the one mounted on it also moves. [Counter:] Because the actions of part and composite have different causes (<s>nimitta</s>). And because the causes are not simultaneous. For when the self's desire to move the hand arises, then there is effort; then from the conjunction of the self possessing effort with the hand, there is action in the hand. But when a particular effort arises in the self for the purpose of moving the body, then from the conjunction of the self possessing that effort with the body, there is action in the body — thus the causes are different. Therefore, since they are different, when one arises, how could the other, whose birth depends on a different cause, also arise in the absence of that [cause]? But for the actions of the chariot and the one mounted on it, even though the causes are different, there is coexistence because the causes are simultaneous. For the push is the non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>) of the chariot's action, while the conjunction with the thing pushed is [the non-inherent cause] of the action of the one mounted on it. And since these two are co-existent, the two actions also arise simultaneously. Having considered all this, the venerable <s>Dharmottara</s> stated this: the part does not have action here. For when the parts have action, separation (<s>vibhāga</s>) arises. Because action is an unrestricted cause with respect to the origination of separation. And when the conjunction that is the non-inherent cause ceases due to that [separation], the composite substance (<s>dravya</s>) would also cease. To this, the followers of <s>Kaṇāda</s> say: the specific action arising from pushing or striking is seen to originate a separation that is the counterpart of the conjunction that produces the substance. But other [action] produces mere separation, not the specific [separation] described. In other actions such as the closing and opening of a lotus, the cessation of the conjunction of parts is not observed. Similarly, even action produced by effort does not have the capacity to bring about the cessation of conjunction. Therefore, there is no destruction of the substance. Here is the resolution of this: when the composite whole has action, its parts must necessarily also have action. Otherwise, there would be separation of the composite whole, which has action, from the regions of space conjoined with the parts, and conjunction with regions not conjoined with the parts. But the parts, being devoid of action, would not depart from the regions of space previously occupied, nor would they come into contact with the regions occupied by the composite whole. And the conjunction and separation of the parts should not be explained through the conjunction and separation of the composite whole, since it is not accepted that the conjunction and separation of the cause are the condition for the conjunction and separation of the effect. For it is only the conjunction and separation of the cause that originate the conjunction and separation of the effect.

body.text:
na ca viparyyayaḥ sidvāntahāniprasaṅgāt / tenāvayavāvayavināṃ pṛthagdeśatvādādhāryyādhārabhāvahānau samavāyo 'pi na vyavatiṣṭheta / tasmādavayavini kriyāvati avayavāḥ kriyāvanta ityakāmakairapi vaiśeṣikairidamabhyupeyaṃ / yathā cāvayavikriyāyāmavayavāḥ kriyāvanta stathāvayaveṣvapi kriyāvatsu tadavayavaiḥ kriyāvadbhirbhāvyamiti / anayā diśā dvyaṇuke kriyāvati tadārambhakau paramāṇūkriyāvantau mantavyau /
ataścalāvayavasambandhinaścalāḥ paramāṇavaḥ / niḥkriyāvayavasambandhinastu niḥkriyā / paramāṇukriyāyāṃ tadārabdhamapi bdyaṇukadravyaṃ kriyāvat prasajyeta / sarvvāvayavakriyāyāḥ kāryyakriyāvinābhūtatvāt / ekasya paramāṇoḥ kriyā na parasyeti cet / sakriyaniḥkriyau tarhi paramāṇū parasparaṃ vibhajyamānāvujjhitadravyārambhakasaṃyogau syātāṃ / tataśca dravyanāśaḥ / evañca bdyaṇukadravyasya kriyāvattve tryaṇuke 'pi kriyā syādityanena krameṇa paridṛśyamāno 'calaścalaḥ syādavayavaḥ / tasmānniḥkriyāvayavasambandhino niḥkriyāḥ paramāṇavaścalāvayavasambandhibhyaścalebhyo vibhajyamānā dravyārambhakasaṃyogavināśavantaḥ syuḥ / niravayavo hi paramāṇuryamaṇumātranabhodeśamākramya paramāṇvantareṇa saṃyujyate / tato vibhajyamānaḥ kathamanujjhitaparamāṇvantarapratyāsattikaḥ syāt / sāvayavo hi bhāva ekenāvayavena vastvantarasaṃyukta evāvayavāntarai ścalaiḥ / pūrvvākrāntānnabhodeśān virahayya deśāntaramākrāmet / niravayaveṣu tvatyantamastamiteyaṃ katheti yuktaṃ drabyanāśaprasaṅgamutpaśyāmaḥ /
body.translated_text:
Nor [can] the reverse [hold], because of the unwanted consequence of abandoning one's own <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine). Since the parts (<s>avayavas</s>) and the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) occupy different locations, if the relation of support and supported is abandoned, even <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) would not be established. Therefore, even the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>, reluctantly, must accept this: that when the composite whole possesses motion (<s>kriyā</s>), its parts possess motion. And just as the parts are in motion when the composite whole is in motion, so too when the parts are in motion, their own sub-parts must also be in motion. In this way, when a <s>dvyaṇuka</s> (dyad) possesses motion, the two <s>paramāṇus</s> (atoms) that constitute it must be considered to possess motion.
Therefore, <s>paramāṇus</s> connected to moving parts are moving; but those connected to motionless parts are motionless. When the <s>paramāṇus</s> are in motion, the <s>dvyaṇuka</s> substance produced by them would also be in motion, since the motion of all parts is invariably concomitant with the motion of the effect. If it is objected that the motion of one <s>paramāṇu</s> is not that of another — then the two <s>paramāṇus</s>, one in motion and one motionless, being separated from each other, would lose the conjunction that produces the substance. And from that, the substance would be destroyed. And if the <s>dvyaṇuka</s> substance possesses motion, then the <s>tryaṇuka</s> (triad) too would possess motion — and by this progression, an observed immovable part would become movable. Therefore, motionless <s>paramāṇus</s> connected to motionless parts, being separated from moving ones connected to moving parts, would undergo the destruction of the conjunction that produces the substance. For the <s>paramāṇu</s>, being partless, occupies an atomic-measure space-point and conjoins with another <s>paramāṇu</s>. When separated from it, how could it retain its proximity to another <s>paramāṇu</s>? For an entity that has parts can, while conjoined with another thing by one part, move to another location by its other moving parts, departing from the previously occupied space-points. But in the case of partless entities, this account has entirely vanished — therefore we see rightly the unwanted consequence of the destruction of the substance.

body.text: athavānyathāyaṃ virudvadharmmasaṃsargaḥ / tathāhyāvṛte ekasmin pāṇyādau sthūlasyārthasyāvṛtānāvṛte rūpe yugapadbhavantī virudvadharmmadvayasaṃyogamasyāvedayataḥ / na cānāvṛtaikarūpa evāyamiti śakyaṃ vaktuṃ / ardvāvaraṇe 'pi anāvṛtasya pūrvvavaddarśanaprasaṅgāt / avayavadarśanāyattopalabdheḥ / taddṛṣṭau asyā dṛṣṭiriti cet / adṛṣṭireva tarhi asyāstu / na tu dṛṣṭayadṛṣṭī / nanvastyevāvayavidarśanamavayavāvaraṇe 'pīti ko 'yaṃ prasaṅgaḥ / evantarhi sthūlaḥ prāgvadupalabhyeta / idamatrāha kaścit / bhūyo 'vayavendriyasannikarṣasahāyo 'vayavīndriyasannikarṣaḥ sthūlopalabdhenimittaṃ, na cārdvāvaraṇe bhūyasāmavayavānāmastīndriyasannikarṣaḥ tato na sthūlagrahaṇamiti / so 'pyevaṃ praṣṭavyaḥ / kiṃ sthūlo nāmāvayavino 'nyaḥ / sa evānekavyāpī sthūlaḥ / tatra yadyavayavyeva sthūlaḥ / tadā tadgrahaṇe kathanna sthūlagrahaṇamiti cintyam /
body.translated_text: Alternatively, there is [another argument:] the co-presence of contradictory properties (<s>viruddhadharmasaṃsarga</s>). For when one thing — such as a hand — covers [part of] a gross object, the covered and uncovered forms arise simultaneously, revealing the conjunction of two contradictory properties. Nor can one say that it has only an uncovered single form, because even in partial covering, there would be the unwanted consequence of seeing the uncovered [whole] as before. The perception [of the uncovered part] depends on the perception of the parts. If it is objected that 'seeing the parts constitutes seeing it' — then let there simply be no seeing of it [the whole]; but do not say that it is both seen and unseen. 'But the composite whole is indeed perceived even when its parts are covered — so what is this unwanted consequence?' If so, then the gross [object] would be perceived as before [even when covered]. To this, someone says the following: 'The sense-contact with the composite whole is aided by the sense-contact with more parts, and this is the cause of perceiving the gross object. In partial covering, there is no sense-contact with the greater number of parts, so there is no apprehension of the gross.' He too should be questioned thus: Is the gross something other than the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>)? Or is it the very same thing, extending over many parts, that is called gross? If the composite whole itself is the gross — then when it is apprehended, how can the apprehension of the gross not occur? This should be considered.

body.text: atha sthūlatvākhyaḥ parimāṇaviśeṣo guṇaḥ sa drabyādanya eveti cet / evantarhi parimāṇarahitameva tat dravyamupa labhyate / na tvasyānyenānyena parimāṇena yogaḥ / na cāsyānekaparimāṇakalpanāpi sādhvī / yugapat sarvveṣāmanupalabdheḥ / na ca dṛśyasya darśananivṛttiryuktā / avayavasyaiva tat parimāṇamupalabhyata iti cet / yadyevaṃ sa eva tarhyavayavaḥ svena parimāṇena sambadvaḥ pratyakṣostvāvaraṇakālenāvayavī / syādetadekārthasamabāyādbhāntinimittādavayavyevāvayavaparimāṇena sambadvaḥ pratibhātīti tadapi na śobhanaṃ / dvayoḥ samaparimāṇayoravayavāvayavinoḥ pratibhāsaprasaṅgaḥ / yasya hi mahato 'vayavasya tata parimāṇaṃ sa tāvat svena parimāṇena sambadvaḥ pratibhāti / avayavinaśca tatparimāṇasambadvapratibhāsābhyupagame dvayoḥ samaparimāṇayorayavāyavavinoḥ pratibhāsa āsajyate /
body.translated_text: If it is said that grossness (<s>sthūlatva</s>) is a particular quality of <s>parimāṇa</s> (magnitude), which is a <s>guṇa</s> (quality), and is distinct from the substance (<s>dravya</s>) — then in that case, the substance itself is perceived without magnitude. Nor is there a connection of this [substance] with any other magnitude. Nor is it proper to attribute to it multiple magnitudes, since all of them are not perceived simultaneously. And it is not reasonable that a visible thing should not be seen. If it is said that it is the magnitude of the part that is perceived — then in that case, it is only the part itself, connected with its own magnitude, that is directly perceived; let the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) exist at the time of covering. It might be said: 'Due to the error caused by inherence in the same object (<s>ekārthasamavāya</s>), the composite whole appears as connected with the magnitude of its parts.' But that too is not sound, because there would be the unwanted consequence of the appearance of two entities — the part and the composite whole — of equal magnitude. For the large part whose magnitude that is, it at least appears connected with its own magnitude. And if one accepts that the composite whole also appears connected with that [same] magnitude, then the appearance of two things — the part and the composite whole — of equal magnitude is entailed.

body.text: na cāsti yathoktaḥ pratibhāsaḥ parimāṇarahitaḥ / so 'vayavaḥ pratibhāsa iti cet / syādetadyasyāvayavasya parimāṇenāvayavī sambadvaḥ pratibhāti sa svaṃ parimāṇaṃ parityajyābhātīti / idamapi parimāṇavirahiṇovayavasyādṛṣṭeraśakyaṃ kalpayituṃ / ekārthasamavāyācca bhrānti nimittādalpatarāvayavaparimāṇavānapyavayavī pratibhāseta / na ca bādhakamantareṇa bhrāntirapi śakyā vyavasthāpayitum /
body.translated_text: If it is said that there is no such appearance as described — that it is the appearance of the part, without magnitude — it might be suggested that the part whose magnitude makes the composite whole appear gives up its own magnitude and appears [without it]. But this too cannot be imagined, since a part devoid of magnitude is not observed. And from the error caused by inherence in the same object, the composite whole might even appear with a lesser magnitude than that of the part. And without a means of refutation (<s>bādhaka</s>), even an erroneous cognition (<s>bhrānti</s>) cannot be determined to be such.

body.text: asti tarhi sthūlo 'vayava eva pratyakṣaḥ / evamāvaraṇakāla ivānāvaraṇāvasthāyāmapi sthūlataro 'vayavaḥ pratyakṣo 'stu / paramadhyāvarttināmavayavānāmindriyasannikarṣābhāve sthūlatamāvayavidarśanānupapatteḥ syānmataṃ nikhilā vayavadarśanaṃ na sthūlapratyakṣakāraṇaṃ / kintu bhūyo 'vayavadarśanamiti / idamapi na samyak / abhimukhāvasthitasya hi parvvatāderarvvācīnāvayavadarśanena tathā sthūlapratipattiryathārvvākparamadhyavarttināṃ darśane / tato na yāvanniravaśeṣāvayavadarśanaṃ tāvat kathaṃ sthūlatamārthapratipattiḥ syāt / na cāvayavā arvākparamadhyavarttino yugapaddṛśyante / tat kathamavayavī sthūlo dṛśyeta / krameṇa diśāmavayavānāṃ pratyakṣīkaraṇe pratyakṣaḥ sthūlo 'vayavīti cet / anyadā tu kaḥ pratyakṣaḥ iti vimṛṣyaṃ / avayava iti cet / avayavī api paramadhyavarttino na yugapaddṛśyanta iti kathaṃ so 'pi pratyakṣaḥ syāt / tadevaṃ nāvayavī nāvayavāḥ pratyakṣā iti na kiñcidṛśyeteti / tat sidvamāvṛtānāvṛtarūpaḥ sthūlo 'rtha iti //
body.translated_text: Therefore, only the gross part itself is directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). Thus, just as at the time of covering, so also in the state of non-covering, let the grosser part be directly perceived. Since when there is no sense-contact with the parts situated at the far end, in the middle, and near end, the perception of the grossest composite whole is impossible — it might be held that the perception of all parts is not the cause of the perception of the gross; rather, the perception of more parts is. But this too is not right. For in the case of a mountain standing in front, the perception of the gross object is the same through the perception of the near parts as through the perception of the parts near, far, and in the middle. Therefore, until there is the perception of all parts without remainder, how can there be the perception of the grossest object? And the parts situated near, far, and in the middle are not seen simultaneously. So how could the composite whole — the gross — be seen? If it is said that through the gradual perception of parts in different directions, the composite whole is perceived as gross — then what is perceived at other times? This should be examined. If [it is said] the part — then the composite whole too does not have its far, middle, and near parts perceived simultaneously, so how could it too be perceived? Thus, neither the composite whole nor the parts are directly perceived — so nothing at all would be seen. Therefore, it is established: the gross object has both covered and uncovered forms.

body.text: tathā rāgārāgābhyāṃ virodhaḥ sambhāvanīyaḥ / tathā hyekasminnukte sthulo 'rtho raktārakte rūpe yugapat pratipadyamāno virudvarūpadvayayogamātmanaḥ prakāśayati / nanva vayava eva rakto 'vayavī tvaraktaikarūpa eveti / yadyevaṃ rakte 'vayave 'raktarūpo 'vayavī dṛśyeta / na caivaṃ / athavā rāgadravyasaṃyogo hi raktatvaṃ / avayavasya ca rāgadravyeṇa saṃyoge 'vayavino 'pi tena bhāvyaṃ / avaśyaṃ hi kāraṇasaṃyoginā kāryyamapi saṃyujyata iti samayāt / yastvāha rakta evāvayavī / asti hi kuṅkumārakte paṭāvayave kuṅkumāraktaḥ paṭa iti pratyayaḥ / tato rāgadravyasaṃyukta evāvayavīti tasyāpi varṇāntarānavabhāsaḥ syādavayavinaḥ / rāgadravyaṃ hi pratyāsīdat nijarūpaṃ vastuna stirodhatte svena ca rūpeṇa dravyaṃ sambandhati / yathā raktovayavastirohitasahajarūpo rāgadravyasamavāyinā rūpeṇa sambandhī pratibhāti / avayavinyapi rāgadravyasaṃyogini varṇāntarānavabhāsaprasaṅgo durvvāraḥ / tanna rakta evāvayavīti śakyaṃ vaktum /
body.translated_text: Similarly, a contradiction through colored and uncolored [properties] can be envisaged. For thus, when a single gross object is stated [to exist], cognizing simultaneously its colored and uncolored forms, it reveals in itself a conjunction of two contradictory forms. [Objection:] It is only the part that is colored; the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) has a single uncolored form. [Reply:] If so, the composite whole, having an uncolored form, would be seen [as uncolored] even when its part is colored. But this is not the case. Or [alternatively]: conjunction with a coloring substance is what constitutes being colored. And when the part has conjunction with a coloring substance, the composite whole too must have it, since it is an established principle that what is conjoined with the cause is necessarily conjoined with the effect as well. But [for] one who says the composite whole is indeed colored: there is the cognition 'a cloth is saffron-colored' when the cloth-part is colored with saffron. Therefore, the composite whole is conjoined with the coloring substance — but then there would also be the unwanted consequence of no appearance of other colors in the composite whole. For a coloring substance, when applied, conceals the inherent color of the thing and connects the substance with its own color. Just as the colored part, whose inherent color is concealed, appears as connected with the color inhering in the coloring substance, so too the unwanted consequence is unavoidable that the composite whole, being conjoined with the coloring substance, would show no appearance of other colors. Therefore, it cannot be said that the composite whole is simply colored.

body.text: anyastu saṃyogasyāvyāpyavṛttyā samādhatte / sa hyāha śabda ivāvyāpyavṛttiḥ saṃyogaḥ / tenaikārtho raktaścāraktaśceti / so 'pyevaṃ paryyanuyojyaḥ / kathamavyāpyavṛttiḥ / yadi hi svāśraye samaveto rūpādivat vyāpyavṛttirevāyaṃ / asamavetaścāvṛttirevāpyadravyeṣtiva gandhaḥ / ekatra saṃyogasyabhāvābhāvāvyāpino vṛttiriti cet / syādetadyathā virudvāvapi rūparasāvekamāśrayete / tathā saṃyogasyāpyekatra bhāvābhāvau yugapat syātām /
body.translated_text: Another [philosopher], however, resolves this through the non-pervading existence (<s>avyāpyavṛtti</s>) of conjunction. He says: conjunction has non-pervading existence, like sound. Therefore, one and the same thing is both colored and uncolored. He too should be questioned thus: how is it non-pervading? For if it inheres (<s>samaveta</s>) in its substrate, it has pervading existence, like color and such. And if it does not inhere, it would simply have no existence, like smell in non-material substances. [Objection:] The existence of conjunction in a single thing, pervading both presence and absence, constitutes [non-pervading existence]. [Reply:] Granted, just as color and taste, though contradictory, share a single substrate, so too the presence and absence of conjunction might simultaneously exist in one thing.

body.text: aho mohavijṛmbhitaṃ / abhāvo hi bhāvanivṛttirūpo nāsya bhāvanivṛttiṃ hitvā rūpāntaramīkṣate / yaśca yannivṛttirūpaḥ sa kathaṃ tasmin satyeva bhavati / bhāve vā tannivṛttirūpatāṃ jahyāt / tathā hyanalaṃ paśyannapi salilārthī tatra pravartteta / jalaviviktasyānalasya daśanāt / jalābhāvasidverapravṛtteriti cet / bhavatvanupalambhājjalābhāvasidvistathāpi jalasattāṃ sambhāvayan jalārthī pravartteta / nanu tatra yadi jalaṃ syādupalabhyeta kimataḥ / ato 'nupalambhādabhāvo jalasyeti / yadyapyabhyupagataiva jalābhāvasidviḥ / tathāpi tadarthinastadbhāvaśaṅkayā pravṛttiḥ syāt / yugapadekatra saṃyogasya bhāvābhāvau dṛśyete / tenaivaṃ kalpayāmo na svecchayā / nanu kimabhāvobhāvapratiṣedhātmakaḥ pratīyate / anyathā vā / tatra bhāvanivṛttirūpe 'bhāve sidve kathaṃ bhāvopalabdhirna bhrāntā syāt / bhāvāpratiṣedhātmakaśca nābhāvaḥ / nāmamātrantu syāt / na ca nāmamātrādarthasya tathābhāvaḥ / rūparasayostu na parasparanivṛttī rūpamiti kathaṃ tadudāharaṇamiha śobheta / na ca rūparasayorekatra samavāyo 'smābhiranu manyate / śabdo 'pyevamevāvyāpyavṛttirasidvaḥ sa kathaṃ prakṛtasaṃśayanivṛttaye kalpyeteti / alaṃ bahubhāṣitayā //
body.translated_text: Oh, what a display of delusion! For non-existence is of the nature of the cessation of existence; apart from the cessation of existence, no other form of it is discerned. And how can that which is of the nature of the cessation of something exist while that very thing exists? Or, if it exists alongside [that thing], it would abandon its nature as that thing's cessation. For then, even someone seeing fire, desiring water, would proceed toward it [the fire] — since one sees fire devoid of water. [Objection:] One would not proceed because the non-existence of water is established through non-apprehension. [Reply:] Let it be so — the non-existence of water is established through non-apprehension. Still, one desiring water, entertaining the possibility of water's existence, would proceed. [Counter:] If water were there, it would be apprehended — what of that? Therefore, from non-apprehension, the absence of water follows. [Reply:] Although the absence of water is accepted, still, due to the suspicion of its existence, one desiring it would proceed. [For your position implies that] the presence and absence of conjunction are simultaneously perceived in one place, and we postulate this accordingly, not by our own wish. [Objection:] Is non-existence cognized as having the nature of the negation of existence, or otherwise? If non-existence in the form of cessation of existence is established, how would the apprehension of existence not be erroneous? And non-existence that is not of the nature of the negation of existence would not be non-existence at all — it would be a mere name. And a thing does not become so merely from a name. [Reply:] As for color and taste, their mutual cessation is not their nature — so how would that analogy be apt here? Nor do we accept the <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) of color and taste in a single substrate. Sound too is similarly unestablished as having non-pervading existence — how could it be postulated to remove the doubt at issue? Enough of verbose discourse!

body.text: athavā sthūlo 'rthastadataddeśaḥ pratīyate / taddeśayośca parasparābhāvāvyabhicāranimitto 'sti virodhaḥ / ato virudvadharmmasaṃsargaḥ sthūlasya / syādetat kathaṃ tadataddeśayoḥ parasparābhāvāvyabhicāraḥ / ucyate / iha tāvadekasmin deśe paricchidyamāne tādrūpyapracyutirasya vyavacchidyate / tadavyavacchede tatparicchedābhāvaprasakteḥ / pracyutivacca pracyutimadapi deśāntaraṃ vyavacchidyate / yadi hi paricchidyamāno deśāntarasvabhāvo bhavettadā tadrūpa evopalabdho bhavet / deśāntararūpantu virahayya svena rūpeṇa prakāśamāno deśo deśāntarāsaṃsṛṣṭa ityavasīyate / yathā ca deśasya deśāntarāsaṃsargastathā tenādhārabhūtena deśena yadyāptaṃ rūpaṃ tadapi deśāntarasaṃsargādavicchinnaṃ bhavati / kathaṃ hi tena deśena vyāptaṃ rūpaṃ tadabhāvavati deśāntare vartteta / yathā ekena deśena vyāpto ghaṭo na deśāntare varttate / deśāntare 'nupalambhādavṛttiriti cet / viprakṛṣṭe deśāntare kathamasyābhāvaḥ pratipattavyaḥ / tasmādidamakāmakenāpi vācyaṃ / yaduta ekadeśavyāptaṃ rūpaṃ na deśāntare varttate iti / tasya tena byāpanaprasaṅgāt / tadabhāvavati deśāntare varttamāno 'pi tena deśena vyāpyeta / na ca vyāptirasya śakyāvasātuṃ / bhāgāntarāsambhavāt / etena tannirastaṃ / yadāha kaścit / yathaikobhāvastadataddeśaṃ janayannavirudhyata iti / tadapi na prakṛtānurūpam /
body.translated_text: Alternatively, the gross object is cognized as having such-and-such a location. And between the two locations ('this location' and 'that location'), there is a contradiction grounded in the invariable non-deviation from the mutual absence of each. Therefore, the gross object has the co-presence of contradictory properties (<s>viruddhadharmasaṃsarga</s>). It might be asked: how is there an invariable non-deviation from the mutual absence between 'this location' and 'that location'? It is answered: here, when one location is delimited, the departure from its identical nature is ascertained. For if that departure were not ascertained, there would be the unwanted consequence that the delimitation of that [location] would not occur. And just as the departure [is ascertained], so too the other location possessing that departure is ascertained. For if the object being delimited were of the nature of another location, then it would be perceived as having that form alone. But the location, appearing in its own form while abandoning the form of another location, is ascertained as not mixed with another location. And just as a location is not mixed with another location, so too the form that pervades that supporting location is unbroken from [its] connection with that other location. For how could a form that pervades a certain location exist in another location where that [first location] is absent? Just as a pot pervaded by one location does not exist in another location. If it is objected: 'Its non-existence in another location is [known] from non-perception' — then how is its absence to be ascertained in a distant location? Therefore, even reluctantly, this must be stated: namely, that a form pervading one location does not exist in another location. Because there would be the unwanted consequence of its pervading that [other location] as well. Even while existing in another location where the first is absent, it would be pervaded by that [first] location. And its pervasion cannot be ascertained, because there is no possibility of [delimiting] another portion. By this, that [view] is also refuted which someone states: 'Just as one entity, while producing such-and-such a location, is not contradicted.' But that too is not appropriate to the matter at hand.

body.text: tathāhi bhāvābhāvāveva parasparaparihāreṇa virudvau na vastunī / vastunostu parasparābhāvāvyabhicāreṇa virodhaḥ / tena yadeva vastu vastvantarapracyutimat tadeva tena virudvaṃ / na caikakāryyanivarttanaśaktiḥ kāryyāntaraśaktayabhāvāvyabhicāriṇī / anupalambho hi vastuno vastvantarābhābāvyabhicāraṃ sādhayati / ekakāryyanirvarttanaśaktimati ca rūpe gṛhyamāṇe kāryyāntara nirvarttanaśaktirapi paricchidyata iti / kathaṃ tadabhāvaḥ / ekadeśasambadvaṃ tu rūpaṃ deśāntarasaṃsargirūpaparihāreṇopalabhyamānantadabhāvāvyabhicāri tena virudvaṃ / yathātyanta sadṛśorvastunoryugapadupalabhyamānayoḥ satyapi cākārabhede dūrādanupalakṣyamāṇabhedayordeśabhedamātranimittakaṃ pratyakṣāvasitaṃ virodhamāśritya bhedo 'vasthāpyate / yastvāha / yathaikaṃ cakṣurvijñānaṃ bhinneṣu cakṣurādiṣu varttate tadadhīnotpādatayā / tathānyo 'pi bhinnadeśanivṛttirnna bhetsyata iti / so 'pi deśabhedanimitte virodhe 'vasthāpyamāne vastunaḥ kāraṇabhedanimittaṃviro dhamāsañjayan na naipuṇyamātmano nivedayati / na hi vijñānasya deśo 'sti kaścit / amūrttatvāt / syādetat / yathā deśabhedanimitto virodhastathā kāraṇabhedanimitto 'pi syāt / ko hi vastuto viśeṣaḥ, kāraṇabhedāddeśabhedasyeti /
body.translated_text: For indeed, it is existence and non-existence alone that are contradictory through mutual exclusion — not [two] real things. But for a real thing, contradiction is through the invariable non-deviation from the mutual absence [of the other]. Therefore, whatever thing possesses the departure from another thing — that very thing is contradicted by it. And the capacity to produce one effect is not invariably non-deviant from the absence of the capacity to produce another effect. For <s>anupalambha</s> (non-apprehension) establishes the invariable non-deviation of a thing from the absence of another thing. But when a form possessing the capacity to produce one effect is apprehended, the capacity to produce another effect is also delimited. So how can there be its absence? But a form connected with one location, being apprehended through the exclusion of a form connected with another location, is invariably non-deviant from the absence of that — and therefore contradicted by it. Just as with two extremely similar things perceived simultaneously — even though there is a difference of form, when the difference is not discernible from a distance — difference is established by relying on the contradiction ascertained by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception), whose sole ground is the difference of location. But whoever says: 'Just as one visual consciousness operates in different sense-organs such as the eye and so forth, because its arising depends on them — so too another [entity] that ceases in different locations would not be differentiated' — he too, when the contradiction grounded in the difference of location is established, while attributing a contradiction grounded in the difference of cause, does not demonstrate his own cleverness. For consciousness has no location whatsoever, since it is immaterial. It might be said: 'Just as there is contradiction grounded in difference of location, so too there could be contradiction grounded in difference of cause. For what real difference is there between difference of location and difference of cause?'

body.text: uktamiha / parasparābhāvāvyabhicāranimitto vastūnāmasti virodhaḥ / sa deśabhede 'pi sannidhīyete na kāraṇabhede / deśabhedavatī hi rūpe 'nyo 'nyaparihāreṇopalabhyamāne / parasparābhāvāvyabhicāriṇī bhavato na kāraṇabhedavatī / tadevaṃ kamparāgāvaraṇabhāvābhāvakṛte deśabhedanibandhane ca caturthe virudvadharmmasaṃsarge 'vayaviviṣaye vyavasthāpite pakṣadharmmatvaṃ sidvaṃ hetoḥ / adhunāvyāptirevāsya svasādhyena samarthanīyā / iha virudvadharmmasaṃsargavirahamātranibandhano bhedavyavahāro vastūnāṃ dṛṣṭaḥ, ahetorayogāt / nimittāntarasya vādarśanāt / tato virudvadharmmasaṃsarge 'pi bhavannabhedavyavahāro vyāpakaṃ nimittavattvaṃ jahyāt / tato vyāpakānupalabdhyā tasmādvyāvṛtto virudvadharmmaviraheṇa vyāpyate / tadvirudvaśca virudvadharmmasaṃsargaḥ / teneyaṃ vyāpakavirudvopalabdhibhūmikā / evaṃ prasādhite 'syāstrairūpye 'sidvavirudvānaikāntikā doṣā nāvakāśaṃ labhante / iti //
body.translated_text: It has been stated here: the contradiction of real things is grounded in the invariable absence of each in the presence of the other. This [contradiction] is present even when there is difference of location, but not when there is difference of cause. For when forms with different locations are apprehended as mutually exclusive, they are invariably accompanied by each other's absence — but not when they merely have different causes. Thus, having established the co-presence of contradictory properties (<s>viruddhadharmasaṃsarga</s>) in the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) through the four [arguments concerning] motion, coloring, covering, and the existence-non-existence [of conjunction] — all grounded in difference of location — the property of the subject (<s>pakṣadharmatva</s>) of the reason (<s>hetu</s>) is established. Now, its pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) with its own thesis to be proven must be demonstrated. Here, the practical convention of difference among things is observed to be grounded solely in the absence of the co-presence of contradictory properties, since without a reason [it would be] impossible, and since no other cause is observed. Therefore, the practical convention of non-difference, even when the co-presence of contradictory properties exists, would abandon its pervading condition of being caused. Therefore, through the non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>), that which is excluded from it [non-difference] is pervaded by the absence of contradictory properties. And the co-presence of contradictory properties is contradictory to that [absence]. Therefore, this is the ground for the apprehension of what is contradictory to the pervader (<s>vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi</s>). With the triple character (<s>trairūpya</s>) of [the reason] thus established, the faults of being unestablished, contradictory, or inconclusive (<s>asiddha-viruddha-anaikāntika</s>) find no scope. Thus it is.

children.text: evaṃ mayā bahuṣu durmmatinirmmiteṣu pratyudvṛteṣu khalu dūṣaṇakaṇṭakeṣu /
children.translated_text: Thus by me, when the many thorns of objections fashioned by those of wrong views have been removed,
this path of the <s>Ācārya</s>'s (master's) logic has been purified — let people, casting aside jealousy, proceed along it.

body.translated_text: Thus is completed this <s>Avayavinirākaraṇa</s> (Refutation of the Composite Whole).
